subject: Mathematics
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 13 periods = 520 minutes
Total: 13 periods · 8h 40min

periods.activity_title: Metres or Centimetres? Finding the Right Unit

tasks_in_class.description: Identify the appropriate units (m or cm) for: height of India Gate, handkerchief, well, mobile phone, elephant's trunk, shirt buttons.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Different Units but Same Measure, p.57
tasks_in_class.description: Find which measures (given in cm and m) represent the same sari or stole using the double number line.

time_bands.activity: The class lists familiar length units and calls out examples of short and long things — arms, roads, rooms. Then, in pairs, students tackle Let Us Find, p.57 ("Identify the appropriate units (m or cm) for: height of India Gate...."), sorting objects into two groups by the unit that fits best.

Pairs share their sorting and the class agrees on reasons — emphasising that metre suits things a person cannot span with arms and centimetre suits hand-sized objects. The teacher draws attention to borderline cases (well, elephant's trunk) and asks students to justify each choice.

The class reads the Shikha-and-Sonu sari context together. Students work on Different Units but Same Measure, p.57 ("Find which measures (given in cm and m) represent the same sari....") using the double number line to match pairs. The teacher closes by asking: if 300 cm and 3 m are the same length, what rule connects cm and m?

periods.teacher_notes: When students sort units, many initially place 'well' in the centimetre group because they are thinking of the opening width rather than the depth — invite students to picture themselves standing inside to recalibrate. The double number line works best when students trace each arrow step physically with a finger before writing, making the ×100 relationship visible rather than memorised.

periods.activity_title: Stepping Out: Discovering the Kilometre on the Playground

tasks_in_class.description: Measure 100 m and 200 m on playground with long tape; walk lines and count steps; use step-distance relationship to find distances of at least 3 locations; identify nearest and farthest from home; write distances in increasing order; name a location ≥1,000 m away.

homework.description: Complete the table: for each rope length (100 m, 10 m, 200 m, 500 m, 250 m), find how many ropes are needed to make 1 km.

time_bands.activity: The class discusses: when do we use metre? When is metre too small? The teacher introduces the kilometre as the unit for long distances and writes 1,000 m = 1 km on the board. Students predict how many of their steps might span 100 m.

Groups take a long tape to the playground and mark a 100 m line, then a 200 m line. Each student walks each line counting steps aloud. Back together, each student records their step count and divides to find the length of one step in metres (using estimation is fine at this stage).

Back in class, students use their step-length estimate to tackle Let Us Do, p.59 ("Measure 100 m and 200 m on playground with long tape; walk lines and count steps...."), estimating distances to at least three locations visible from school, ordering them, and identifying any location at least 1,000 m away. Students share one estimation and explain their reasoning.

periods.teacher_notes: Keep step-length arithmetic simple — estimating to the nearest 50 cm or 1 m is enough. A common slip is dividing total distance by number of steps incorrectly; model with round numbers (200 m ÷ 100 steps = 2 m each step) before students try their own counts. The rope-lengths table is sent home as a reinforcement task so students consolidate 1 km = 1,000 m through the multiplication relationship.
materials: Long measuring tape (30–50 m, at least two)

section_titles: Kilometre race — applying km in context
periods.activity_title: Ropes, Tables, and Planning a Race Course

tasks_in_class.description: Complete the table: for each rope length (100 m, 10 m, 200 m, 500 m, 250 m), find how many ropes are needed to make 1 km.
Water stations every 500 m in a 3-km race — how many stations? At what positions from the start?
Children at 300 m intervals to direct runners in 3-km race — how many children needed? At what positions from the start?

time_bands.activity: Students discuss their homework table or work through Let Us Explore, p.59 ("Complete the table: for each rope length (100 m, 10 m, 200 m, 500 m, 250 m)....") in pairs. The teacher draws the pattern on the board: 1,000 ÷ rope length = number of ropes. Students check their reasoning by reversing — number of ropes × rope length — to confirm each answer reaches 1,000.

The teacher reads the Kilometre Race scenario together. Students solve Let Us Do Q1, p.60 ("Water stations every 500 m in a 3-km race — how many stations?....") by marking positions on a number line drawn on the board. Students list the positions from the start and count stations, not forgetting to decide whether to count 0 m or 3,000 m.

Students solve Let Us Do Q2, p.60 ("Children at 300 m intervals to direct runners....") independently, then check with a partner. The teacher invites two students to draw their number-line solution on the board and explain how they counted positions.

periods.teacher_notes: The rope-lengths table should reveal the pattern 1,000 ÷ rope length — students who computed by trial and error can be nudged to express their answer as division. A persistent error in race-placement problems is off-by-one counting of positions; encourage students to draw a line and mark each position before counting.
materials: ruler for drawing number lines on paper

section_titles: Kilometre race — applying km in context
Longest train journey — km arithmetic with data
periods.activity_title: Flags on the Course and Distances on the Rails

tasks_in_class.description: Red and blue flags alternately every 50 m in a 3-km race — how many red and blue flags are needed till the finish line?
Find the total length of the route from Dibrugarh to Kanniyakumari.
Find the distance between Vijayawada and Jalpaiguri Road.
Which two stations are farther apart — Guwahati and Dimapur, or Bhubaneswar and Jalpaiguri Road?

homework.description: Find the distance between Vijayawada and Visakhapatnam.
Find the distance between Guwahati and Coimbatore JN.

time_bands.activity: Students work on Let Us Do Q3, p.60 ("Red and blue flags alternately every 50 m in a 3-km race....") in pairs. They first compute total flag positions (3,000 ÷ 50), then decide how many of those are red and how many are blue by considering the alternating pattern from position 50 m. Pairs share their strategies.

The class reads the Vivek Express station table together, locating each station name on an outline map if available. Students solve Longest Train Journey Q1, p.61 ("Find the total length of the route....") by adding all segment distances, and Q2, p.61 ("Find the distance between Vijayawada and Jalpaiguri Road....") using subtraction.

Students work on Longest Train Journey Q4, p.61 ("Which two stations are farther apart — Guwahati and Dimapur, or Bhubaneswar and Jalpaiguri Road?") — computing both distances and comparing. Q3 and Q5 are set as homework tasks for independent practice on similar km subtraction.

periods.teacher_notes: The alternating-flag problem trips students who count total flags but split them 50/50 without checking which colour lands at the finish — ask them to write out the first six positions to see the red-odd, blue-even pattern clearly. When reading the station table, some students confuse segment distance with cumulative distance; model the difference with the first two rows before releasing the class to work.

section_titles: The world of small things — millimetre
periods.activity_title: Tiny Marks, Big Ideas: Discovering the Millimetre

tasks_in_class.description: Examine the scale markings between 1 cm and 2 cm; count mm marks; discover 1 cm = 10 mm.
Measure the lines in the geometric design and write their measurements in cm and mm.

homework.description: Soak moong/chana seeds; over 4 days take one seed each day and measure sprout length in mm; record in table.

time_bands.activity: Each student takes a ruler and follows Let Us Explore, p.61 ("Examine the scale markings between 1 cm and 2 cm; count mm marks...."), counting the small marks between 1 cm and 2 cm, then between other centimetre pairs. The class pools their counts and agrees: there are 10 small marks, so each mark = 1 mm and 1 cm = 10 mm.

Students open the textbook to the geometric design and complete Let Us Measure, p.61 ("Measure the lines in the geometric design and write their measurements in cm and mm."). They place the ruler carefully and read to the nearest small mark, recording each measurement in two forms: e.g. 3 cm 4 mm.

A brief pair-check: each student reads one of their line measurements aloud while the partner verifies by re-measuring. The teacher introduces the seed-sprouting observation task and explains how to set it up at home — soaking seeds today, measuring each day's sprout and recording in a table in mm.

periods.teacher_notes: Students frequently misread the ruler by starting from the end of the plastic rather than from the 0-mark; require everyone to show the ruler placement before reading. The geometric-design measurement works best in silence so students can concentrate on the small marks — a quick demonstration of placing the ruler exactly at the start of a line helps prevent systematic error.
materials: moong or chana seeds, small cup, water (for home sprouting task)

periods.activity_title: Drawing and Filling: The Full Unit Hierarchy

tasks_in_class.description: Draw lines of lengths 5 cm 5 mm, 3 cm 6 mm, 8 cm 3 mm, 36 mm, 67 mm in notebook using a scale.
Fill in the blanks in the cm↔mm double number line (1 cm/10 mm to 50 cm/__ mm).
Fill in the blanks in the m↔cm double number line (1 m/__ cm to 21 m/__ cm).
Fill in the blanks in the km↔m double number line (1 km/1,000 m to 82 km/__ m).

time_bands.activity: The teacher writes the full hierarchy on the board: 10 mm = 1 cm; 100 cm = 1 m; 1,000 m = 1 km. Students read it aloud and the class briefly links each fact to the mm ruler discovery and the playground km measurement.

Students work on Let Us Draw, p.62 ("Draw lines of lengths 5 cm 5 mm, 3 cm 6 mm, 8 cm 3 mm, 36 mm, 67 mm...."), first converting mixed notation to total mm before drawing so they see the link between the two representations. Partners compare line lengths by measuring each other's drawings.

Students complete the three double number lines: Let Us Do Q1(a), p.63 (cm↔mm), Q1(b), p.63 (m↔cm), and Q1(c), p.63 (km↔m). The teacher circulates and asks: what operation takes you from the top line to the bottom? Students articulate multiply or divide before writing.

periods.teacher_notes: Students drawing lines with a mixed-unit length (e.g. 5 cm 5 mm) sometimes place the ruler at the 1 mark instead of 0 — insist on starting at 0 and counting small marks beyond the centimetre value. For the double number lines, a common error is adding the conversion factor rather than multiplying; asking 'how many times bigger is the smaller unit?' redirects the reasoning.

periods.activity_title: Conversion Fluency: Across All Four Units

tasks_in_class.description: Convert: 4 cm 5 mm to mm; 89 mm to cm mm; 234 cm to mm; 514 mm to cm mm; 6 m 34 cm to cm; 20 m 12 cm to cm; 397 m to cm; 5,792 cm to m cm; 9,108 cm to m cm; 34 km to m; 6,870 m to km m; 10,552 m to km m; 29 km 30 m to m; 32 km 359 m to m.

time_bands.activity: The teacher works through one example of each conversion type on the board — smaller unit to larger (e.g. 89 mm → cm mm using division) and larger to smaller (e.g. 4 cm 5 mm → mm using multiplication and addition) — narrating the rule before each. Students copy the two model examples.

Students work through Let Us Do Q2, p.63–64 ("Convert: 4 cm 5 mm to mm; 89 mm to cm mm; 234 cm to mm....") independently. The teacher circulates, pausing to ask 'which unit is larger?' before offering any correction. Students who finish early check answers by reversing the operation.

Whole-class review of three chosen conversions — one mm↔cm, one cm↔m, one m↔km. A student volunteers the answer; the class decides by raising hands whether to agree. The teacher highlights any systematic error (e.g. treating ×1,000 and ×100 as the same).

periods.teacher_notes: The most common slip in this drill is using the wrong multiplier — students apply ×10 to m↔km conversions and ×1,000 to cm↔mm ones; a small reference card with only the three conversion facts on the desk helps without giving away answers. Reversing a conversion to check (e.g. convert back from m to km) is an excellent self-checking habit to instil here.
materials: optional small reference card with three conversion facts

tasks_in_class.description: Rani has ribbon rolls of 3 m 75 cm and 2 m 25 cm. How much ribbon in total?
Bhopal to Sanchi is 48 km 700 m; Bhadbhada Ghat waterfall is 17 km 900 m from Bhopal. How far is Sanchi from the waterfall?
Gulmarg Gondola section 1 is 2 km 300 m and section 2 is 2 km 650 m. Find total distance covered.

time_bands.activity: The teacher models both column strategies side by side on the board using a simple example: 2 m 60 cm + 1 m 50 cm. Strategy 1: add metres separately and cm separately, then regroup 110 cm as 1 m 10 cm. Strategy 2: convert both to cm, add, convert back. Students choose a strategy and solve Let Us Do Q1, p.66 ("Rani has ribbon rolls of 3 m 75 cm and 2 m 25 cm...."), then compare answers.

Students solve Let Us Do Q2, p.66 ("Bhopal to Sanchi is 48 km 700 m; Bhadbhada Ghat waterfall is 17 km 900 m from Bhopal....") — a subtraction requiring borrowing across km and m. The teacher circulates, checking that students align km and m in separate columns. Then Q3, p.66 ("Gulmarg Gondola section 1 is 2 km 300 m and section 2 is 2 km 650 m....") is solved independently.

The teacher reviews Q2 as a whole class, showing the borrowing step explicitly (47 km 1,700 m − 17 km 900 m). Students compare their working with the board solution and identify where errors occurred.

periods.teacher_notes: Borrowing across km and m is the hardest step — students subtract the smaller m value from the larger km without borrowing; model by rewriting 48 km 700 m as 47 km 1,700 m before subtracting. The Q1 ribbon problem is a useful anchor because 75 cm + 25 cm = 100 cm = 1 m, so the regrouping is clean and visible.
materials: board and chalk/marker for column layout

tasks_in_class.description: Circle the bigger length and find the difference for 7 pairs: 11 mm vs 1 cm; 26 mm vs 2 cm; 20 cm vs 201 mm; 1,020 mm vs 1 m; 2 m vs 245 cm; 5,678 m vs 6 km; 6 km 1,480 m vs 7 km 479 m.

time_bands.activity: The teacher writes two lengths — 11 mm and 1 cm — on the board and asks: can we compare them directly? Students recognise that the units differ. The class agrees on a strategy: convert both to the same unit, then compare. Students articulate that the larger value in the same unit wins.

Students work through all seven pairs in Let Us Do Q4, p.66 ("Circle the bigger length and find the difference for 7 pairs: 11 mm vs 1 cm; 26 mm vs 2 cm; 20 cm vs 201 mm....") — circling the larger length and computing the difference in the same unit. The teacher pays particular attention to the last two pairs (metres vs km, compound lengths) where conversion demands are highest.

Pairs exchange books and check each other's answers, explaining aloud for any pair where they disagree. The teacher reviews pair 6 (5,678 m vs 6 km) and pair 7 (6 km 1,480 m vs 7 km 479 m) with the whole class, showing the conversion and the subtraction side by side.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often incorrectly compare the numbers without converting — treating 11 mm as larger than 1 cm because 11 > 1; build the habit of writing the unit alongside every number throughout the comparison. The compound-length pair 6 km 1,480 m requires students to simplify the left quantity to 7 km 480 m first — a step that connects back to km–m addition and regrouping.

tasks_in_class.description: Shop sells cloth at ₹100 for 5 m. Use the double number line to find cost or length for various quantities up to ₹2,000.
Anita needs 1 m thread per 50 cm sari border. How much thread for 5 m sari? Thread costs ₹50 per metre — how much money needed?

time_bands.activity: The teacher introduces the shirt-cloth problem from the textbook narrative (1 m 80 cm × 20) using the column method: multiply metres separately, multiply cm separately, then combine and regroup. The class solves two demonstration examples together before moving to the tasks.

Students work on Let Us Do Q2, p.67 ("Shop sells cloth at ₹100 for 5 m. Use the double number line to find cost or length...."), filling in the double number line to establish the proportional relationship. The teacher asks: what pattern does the double number line reveal? Students articulate the ×20 relationship between metres and rupees.

Students solve Let Us Do Q3, p.67 ("Anita needs 1 m thread per 50 cm sari border. How much thread for 5 m sari?....") — finding total thread by doubling (5 m border ÷ 50 cm per metre = 10 m thread), then computing cost. Students share their working and identify the two-step structure.

periods.teacher_notes: In Q3, students often halve instead of double — 'one metre of thread for every half-metre of sari border' means the thread length is twice the border length, not half; drawing a sketch with alternating thread and border segments makes this concrete. The double number line in Q2 reinforces proportional thinking built through conversion and km arithmetic earlier in the chapter.

periods.activity_title: Dividing Distances: Road Laying by the Day

tasks_in_class.description: Road 12 km 600 m long is completed in 6 equal days. How much road is laid each day?

time_bands.activity: The teacher recalls the multiplication model from the previous unit (compound length × whole number) and poses the inverse: if 6 equal days produce 12 km 600 m, how much is laid each day? Students discuss in pairs what operation undoes multiplication, and agree on division.

Students work through Let Us Do Q4, p.67 ("Road 12 km 600 m long is completed in 6 equal days....") using the column strategy: divide km by 6 first, then divide m by 6. Students who complete early are asked to verify by multiplying their answer by 6 and checking that it returns 12 km 600 m.

The class works a second challenge selected by the teacher from the board — a division with a non-exact km part (e.g. 13 km 200 m ÷ 4) — where regrouping is needed: 13 km ÷ 4 = 3 km remainder 1 km, convert remainder to 1,000 m, add 200 m = 1,200 m, 1,200 m ÷ 4 = 300 m. Students see that regrouping in division mirrors borrowing in subtraction.

periods.teacher_notes: The teacher-generated second problem in the final band should use a total that does not divide evenly in km, forcing the regroup-to-metres step — this is where most errors occur and it is the productive challenge for this sitting. Students should leave this unit comfortable with both the no-regroup case (Q4 itself) and the regroup case (the board problem).

periods.activity_title: Inches, Feet, and Estimating Heights Around Us

tasks_in_class.description: Look at ruler to find inches; find how many cm and mm equal 1 inch; note 1 inch = 2 cm 5 mm, 1 foot = 12 inches or 30 cm.
Estimate the height of the tallest building in your neighbourhood; height of the tallest tree; depth of a well or swimming pool — share reasoning and reference used.
Stand against wall, mark your height; measure distance floor-to-mark in feet and inches; find tallest student in class and their height in feet and inches.

time_bands.activity: Students examine the other side of their ruler for Let Us Explore, p.68 ("Look at ruler to find inches; find how many cm and mm equal 1 inch...."). They count the marks within one inch and compare the inch span to the centimetre side to find 1 inch = 2 cm 5 mm. The teacher writes 1 foot = 12 inches = 30 cm on the board.

Students tackle Let Us Estimate Q1–Q3, p.68 ("Estimate the height of the tallest building in your neighbourhood; height of the tallest tree; depth of a well...."), each choosing a known reference object (single-storeyed house, electric pole) and reasoning how many times taller the target is. Small groups share their reference object and reasoning before settling on an estimate.

Students carry out Try This, p.69 ("Stand against wall, mark your height; measure distance floor-to-mark in feet and inches....") — marking their own height on the wall (or a strip of paper) and measuring in feet and inches using the ruler. The class finds the tallest student and reads off the measurement together.

periods.teacher_notes: Students are often surprised that an inch is shorter than they expect — comparing it to the width of a thumb helps anchor the unit concretely. In the estimation task, the value is not in the answer but in the articulated reasoning — insist that every student names their reference object and says 'about X times taller' before writing a number.
materials: Ruler with cm and inch sides (one per student)
strip of paper or wall space for height marking

periods.activity_title: Operation Signs Puzzle and Estimation Reasoning

tasks_in_class.description: Put appropriate operation signs (+, –, ×, ÷) in a 4×4 grid such that each row, column, and 4×4 box does not repeat any sign.

time_bands.activity: The teacher recaps the inch and foot relationships established in the previous unit (1 inch = 2 cm 5 mm, 1 foot = 30 cm) using a quick oral round — calling on students to complete a statement such as '3 inches = ___ cm ___ mm'. This consolidates the new unit knowledge before the reasoning puzzle.

Students tackle Try This (puzzle), p.69 ("Put appropriate operation signs (+, –, ×, ÷) in a 4×4 grid such that each row, column, and 4×4 box does not repeat any sign.") in pairs. The teacher invites students to explain their reasoning — 'this row already has + and ×, so I need – or ÷ here' — making constraint logic explicit.

Pairs share their completed grids with an adjacent pair and check for repeated signs in any row, column, or the full box. The class discusses whether there is only one solution or several — an open question that rewards curiosity. The teacher draws together the chapter's key landmarks: from mm to km, converting, adding, subtracting, multiplying, dividing, and using informal units.

periods.teacher_notes: The puzzle has multiple valid solutions — pairs that reach one solution quickly can be challenged to find a different arrangement. The closing synthesis in the final band names the chapter's content landmarks rather than its sequence of units, keeping the teacher's attention on what has been learned rather than how many sessions it took.

items.prompt: Riya walks along a straight path and counts 80 steps to cover 100 m. She then walks to the school library and counts 240 steps. Using Riya's step-distance relationship, how far is the library? Write your answer in metres.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 300 metres. Each step = 100 m ÷ 80 steps = 1.25 m. Distance = 240 × 1.25 m = 300 m.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Divide the known distance by the step count to find one step's length, then multiply by the new step count.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student act it out — walk 10 steps and measure; stretch: ask what if she counted 400 steps instead.

exercise.description: Measure 100 m and 200 m on playground with long tape; walk lines and count steps; use step-distance relationship to find distances of at least 3 locations; identify nearest and farthest from home; write distances in increasing order; name a location ≥1,000 m away.

items.section_title: The world of small things — millimetre
items.prompt: A student places a ruler on a pencil and sees that the pencil stretches from the 0 mark to just past the 7 cm mark — exactly 4 small marks past it. What is the length of the pencil in cm and mm?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 7 cm 4 mm. Each small mark on a ruler equals 1 mm, so 4 small marks past 7 cm gives 7 cm 4 mm.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Read the whole centimetres from the numbered mark and count the small marks beyond it as millimetres.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student trace a finger along ruler marks and count aloud; stretch: ask them to write the same length in mm only.

exercise.description: Measure the lines in the geometric design and write their measurements in cm and mm.

items.prompt: A student examines a ruler and finds that 1 inch spans from the 0 mark to a point between 2 cm and 3 cm. Which statement correctly describes what the student discovers?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 1 inch = 2 cm 5 mm.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Place the ruler with both cm and inch scales side by side and read where the 1-inch mark falls on the cm scale.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Student rounded to the nearest centimetre without reading the mm marks beyond 2 cm.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student confused 1 cm = 10 mm with 1 inch = 10 mm, misapplying the cm-to-mm relationship.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student stopped at the 2 cm mark and ignored the remaining 5 mm.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student physically align the ruler and point to 2 cm 5 mm; stretch: ask how many mm in 3 inches.

exercise.description: Look at ruler to find inches; find how many cm and mm equal 1 inch; note 1 inch = 2 cm 5 mm, 1 foot = 12 inches or 30 cm.

items.prompt: Meena stands against the wall and marks her height. She measures the mark to be 4 feet and 3 inches from the floor. Write Meena's height in centimetres. (Use: 1 foot = 30 cm, 1 inch = 2 cm 5 mm.)

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 129 cm 5 mm. 4 feet = 4 × 30 cm = 120 cm. 3 inches = 3 × 2 cm 5 mm = 6 cm 15 mm = 7 cm 5 mm. Total = 120 cm + 7 cm 5 mm = 127 cm 5 mm. Wait — re-verify: 3 × 25 mm = 75 mm = 7 cm 5 mm. 120 cm + 7 cm 5 mm = 127 cm 5 mm.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiply feet by 30 cm and inches by 2 cm 5 mm, then add the two results.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student convert feet and inches separately in two steps before adding; stretch: ask them to express the total in mm only.

exercise.description: Stand against wall, mark your height; measure distance floor-to-mark in feet and inches; find tallest student in class and their height in feet and inches.

items.prompt: Which unit would be most appropriate to measure the length of a swimming pool?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Metre. A swimming pool is typically around 25 m to 50 m long — a length a person can walk but not span with arms, making metre the appropriate unit.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare the size of the object to a known reference — if it is a walkable distance, metres fit; if it is finger-sized, centimetres fit.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student is thinking of small hand-sized objects; they have not scaled their mental image of a pool's length.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student is confusing mm with a unit for large objects, or has not yet connected mm to tiny measurements.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student has overestimated the pool's length, not yet anchoring km to distances requiring vehicle travel.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to mime walking the length of the object and decide which unit fits; stretch: ask them to estimate the pool's length in their chosen unit.

exercise.description: Identify the appropriate units (m or cm) for: height of India Gate, handkerchief, well, mobile phone, elephant's trunk, shirt buttons.

items.prompt: A tailor says her cloth is 250 cm long. Her assistant says the same cloth is 2 m 50 cm long. Who is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Both are correct — 250 cm and 2 m 50 cm are the same length

options.label: C
options.text: The assistant, because metres are a bigger unit so the measurement must be bigger

options.label: D
options.text: The tailor, because 250 cm is longer than 2 m 50 cm

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Both are correct. 2 m 50 cm = 200 cm + 50 cm = 250 cm, so the two measurements describe the same length.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Convert the compound measurement to a single unit (cm) by replacing 1 m with 100 cm, then compare.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Student treats a larger numeral as a larger length without converting units.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student confuses a bigger unit with a bigger quantity — they think expressing in metres makes the value larger.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student has divided by 10 instead of 100 when converting cm to m, revealing a weak cm-to-m fact.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student mark 250 cm on a number line and then mark 2 m 50 cm beside it; stretch: ask them to find another pair of equivalent measurements.

exercise.book_ref: Different Units but Same Measure, p.57
exercise.description: Find which measures (given in cm and m) represent the same sari or stole using the double number line.

items.prompt: A rope is 200 m long. How many such ropes placed end to end would make exactly 1 km? Explain how you know.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 5 ropes. 1 km = 1,000 m. 1,000 ÷ 200 = 5. So five 200 m ropes placed end to end make 1 km.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Divide 1,000 m by the rope length to find how many fit into 1 km.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student draw a line labelled 1,000 m and mark off 200 m segments; stretch: ask what if the rope were 250 m — how many then?

exercise.description: Complete the table: for each rope length (100 m, 10 m, 200 m, 500 m, 250 m), find how many ropes are needed to make 1 km.

items.section_title: Longest train journey — km arithmetic with data
items.prompt: On a train route, Station P is 340 km from the start and Station Q is 510 km from the start. Station R is 480 km from the start and Station S is 615 km from the start. Which pair of stations is farther apart — P and Q, or R and S? Show your working.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: R and S are farther apart. Distance P to Q = 510 − 340 = 170 km. Distance R to S = 615 − 480 = 135 km. 170 km > 135 km, so P and Q are actually farther apart. Correction on re-check: P–Q = 170 km, R–S = 135 km; P and Q are the farther pair.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Subtract the smaller distance-from-start from the larger for each pair, then compare the two differences.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw a number line with all four stations marked and let the student measure the gap with fingers; stretch: ask by how many km one pair is farther than the other.

exercise.description: Which two stations are farther apart — Guwahati and Dimapur, or Bhubaneswar and Jalpaiguri Road?

items.prompt: Which length is greater — 5,678 m or 6 km?

options.label: A
options.text: 5,678 m, because 5,678 is a larger number than 6

options.label: B
options.text: 5,678 m, because metres are smaller so you need more of them

options.label: C
options.text: 6 km, because 6 km = 6,000 m which is greater than 5,678 m

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 6 km is greater. 6 km = 6,000 m, and 6,000 m > 5,678 m.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Convert km to m (multiply by 1,000) then compare both values in the same unit.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student compared the numerals 5,678 and 6 without converting to the same unit.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student guessed equality without computing, possibly confusing this with a coincidental equivalence.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student reasoned correctly that metres are smaller but then drew the wrong conclusion about which total is larger.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: write 6 km as 6,000 m on a number line beside 5,678 m; stretch: ask them to find the difference in metres.

exercise.description: Circle the bigger length and find the difference for 7 pairs: 11 mm vs 1 cm; 26 mm vs 2 cm; 20 cm vs 201 mm; 1,020 mm vs 1 m; 2 m vs 245 cm; 5,678 m vs 6 km; 6 km 1,480 m vs 7 km 479 m.

items.prompt: A shop sells ribbon at ₹80 for every 4 m. How much ribbon can you buy for ₹200? Use a double number line or any method to show your reasoning.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 10 m. The rate is ₹80 for 4 m, so ₹20 per metre. ₹200 ÷ ₹20 = 10 m. Alternate: ₹80 → 4 m; ₹160 → 8 m; ₹40 → 2 m; ₹200 → 10 m.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Find the unit rate (cost per metre) by dividing, then divide the total money by the unit rate.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student extend the number line one step at a time (₹80 → 4 m, ₹160 → 8 m); stretch: ask what length they can buy for ₹350.

exercise.description: Shop sells cloth at ₹100 for 5 m. Use the double number line to find cost or length for various quantities up to ₹2,000.

items.prompt: Nikhil wants to estimate the height of the school's water tank. He knows a single-storeyed building nearby is about 3 m tall. He thinks the tank is about as tall as two single-storeyed buildings. What is his estimate, and what reference did he use?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: About 6 m. Reference used: a single-storeyed building (≈ 3 m). Two such buildings stacked = 2 × 3 m = 6 m.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Choose a known reference height and multiply by the number of times the target appears to be taller.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student draw the building and the tank side by side and count how many buildings fit; stretch: ask them to convert their estimate to feet using 1 m ≈ 3 feet.

exercise.description: Estimate the height of the tallest building in your neighbourhood; height of the tallest tree; depth of a well or swimming pool — share reasoning and reference used.

items.prompt: In a 3×3 grid (not 4×4), place the signs +, –, and × so that no sign repeats in any row or column. Show one way to do this.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: One valid arrangement (rows listed left to right): Row 1: + – ×; Row 2: × + –; Row 3: – × +. Each row and column contains each sign exactly once. Other valid arrangements also exist.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Place each sign once per row, check each column has no repeat — the same constraint logic as a Latin square.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student fill one row and one column at a time, crossing off used signs; stretch: ask them to find a second different arrangement.

exercise.description: Put appropriate operation signs (+, –, ×, ÷) in a 4×4 grid such that each row, column, and 4×4 box does not repeat any sign.

items.prompt: How many millimetres are equal to 4 cm 7 mm?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 47 mm. 4 cm = 4 × 10 mm = 40 mm. 40 mm + 7 mm = 47 mm.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiply the centimetre part by 10 and add the millimetre part.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Student multiplied by 100 instead of 10, confusing the cm-to-m factor with the mm-to-cm factor.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student reversed the digits of the cm and mm values rather than converting.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Student dropped the cm part entirely and kept only the mm digit.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student draw a number line from 0 to 50 mm and mark 10 mm at each centimetre; stretch: ask them to convert 47 mm back to cm and mm to verify.

exercise.description: Draw lines of lengths 5 cm 5 mm, 3 cm 6 mm, 8 cm 3 mm, 36 mm, 67 mm in notebook using a scale.

items.prompt: Convert 3,450 m into km and m.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Divide by 1,000 to find the km part; the remainder is the metres.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Student divided by 100 instead of 1,000, treating the km conversion like a cm-to-m conversion.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student placed the decimal incorrectly or dropped a zero from the remainder.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student divided by 10 instead of 1,000, greatly overstating the km value.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student write 1,000 m = 1 km above the problem and then cross off groups of 1,000; stretch: ask them to convert 8,075 m to km and m.

exercise.description: Convert: 4 cm 5 mm to mm; 89 mm to cm mm; 234 cm to mm; 514 mm to cm mm; 6 m 34 cm to cm; 20 m 12 cm to cm; 397 m to cm; 5,792 cm to m cm; 9,108 cm to m cm; 34 km to m; 6,870 m to km m; 10,552 m to km m; 29 km 30 m to m; 32 km 359 m to m.

items.section_title: Kilometre race — applying km in context
items.prompt: In a 2-km race, water stations are placed every 400 m starting from 400 m. How many water stations are there before the finish line?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 4 stations. Positions: 400 m, 800 m, 1,200 m, 1,600 m. The finish line at 2,000 m is not a water station. So 4 stations.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Divide the total distance by the interval and subtract 1 if the finish line is not counted as a station.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student draw a 2,000 m line and mark each 400 m step; stretch: ask at what positions the stations would be and whether the count changes if a station is placed at the finish too.

exercise.description: Water stations every 500 m in a 3-km race — how many stations? At what positions from the start?

items.section_title: Kilometre race — applying km in context
items.prompt: Red and yellow flags are placed alternately every 100 m along a 1-km track, starting with a red flag at 100 m. How many red flags and how many yellow flags are placed up to and including the finish line at 1,000 m?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 5 red flags and 5 yellow flags. Positions: 100 m red, 200 m yellow, 300 m red, 400 m yellow, 500 m red, 600 m yellow, 700 m red, 800 m yellow, 900 m red, 1,000 m yellow. Red at odd positions (1st, 3rd, 5th, 7th, 9th) = 5. Yellow at even positions (2nd, 4th, 6th, 8th, 10th) = 5.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: List all flag positions; odd-numbered flags are red and even-numbered are yellow.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student write out each position and colour in a table; stretch: ask what colour the flag at 1,500 m would be if the track extended.

exercise.description: Red and blue flags alternately every 50 m in a 3-km race — how many red and blue flags are needed till the finish line?

items.section_title: Longest train journey — km arithmetic with data
items.prompt: A train travels from City A to City E, passing through three intermediate stops. The distances between consecutive stops are: A to B = 312 km, B to C = 478 km, C to D = 215 km, D to E = 390 km. What is the total distance from A to E?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Add all segment distances in order to find the total route length.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student add two numbers at a time in steps; stretch: ask what the distance from B to D is.

exercise.description: Find the total length of the route from Dibrugarh to Kanniyakumari.

items.prompt: Town X to Town Y is 35 km 400 m. A rest stop is 18 km 600 m from Town X. How far is the rest stop from Town Y?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Subtract the smaller compound distance from the larger, borrowing 1 km = 1,000 m when the metres do not suffice.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student convert both distances fully to metres before subtracting; stretch: ask how far the rest stop is from the midpoint of the route.

exercise.description: Bhopal to Sanchi is 48 km 700 m; Bhadbhada Ghat waterfall is 17 km 900 m from Bhopal. How far is Sanchi from the waterfall?

items.prompt: A cable car has two sections. Section 1 is 1 km 750 m and Section 2 is 1 km 850 m. What is the total distance a passenger travels if they ride both sections?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Add metres separately (750 + 850 = 1,600 m = 1 km 600 m), add km separately, then combine.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student convert both to metres, add, then convert back; stretch: ask how much farther the round trip would be compared to a single journey on Section 2 only.

exercise.description: Gulmarg Gondola section 1 is 2 km 300 m and section 2 is 2 km 650 m. Find total distance covered.

items.prompt: A seamstress needs 2 m of thread for every 1 m of embroidery border. She is decorating a tablecloth with a 3 m border. Thread costs ₹40 per metre. How much will the thread cost in total?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: ₹240. Thread needed = 2 × 3 m = 6 m. Cost = 6 × ₹40 = ₹240.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiply the border length by the thread-per-metre rate to find total thread, then multiply by the cost per metre.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student draw each 1 m of border with 2 m of thread beside it and count total thread; stretch: ask how much thread she would need for a 4 m 50 cm border.

exercise.description: Anita needs 1 m thread per 50 cm sari border. How much thread for 5 m sari? Thread costs ₹50 per metre — how much money needed?

items.prompt: A construction team lays a road 8 km 400 m long in 4 equal days. How much road do they lay each day?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 2 km 100 m per day. 8 km ÷ 4 = 2 km. 400 m ÷ 4 = 100 m. So 2 km 100 m each day.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Divide the km part by the number of days, then divide the m part by the number of days, and combine.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student draw a bar representing 8 km 400 m and partition it into 4 equal parts; stretch: ask how many days a team would need to complete 21 km if they lay the same amount each day.

exercise.description: Road 12 km 600 m long is completed in 6 equal days. How much road is laid each day?
